description: Authenticated 43rd–44th Congress enacted-law dispositions. Notes are exact target-specific amendments or freestanding continuing statutory provisions, not speculative changes to adjacent U.S. Code sections.

notes.heading: Combatant Command Purge Act—Amendment to Pub. L. 16–116
paragraphs: Pub. L. 43–275, §§ 4–5, amends §§ 5–6 of Pub. L. 16–116 (Combatant Command Re-establishment Act), not 10 U.S.C. § 161. The definitions in Pub. L. 43–275, § 2, cite this section for background only.

As amended, Pub. L. 16–116, § 5(a), establishes United States Special Operations Command as the sole listed unified combatant command, and § 5(b) prohibits new commands or disbanding or redesignating existing commands except by Act of Congress.

As amended, Pub. L. 16–116, § 6, requires combatant commanders to report directly to the Secretary of Defense and permits the Secretary to designate an operational commander for special multibranch military operations, with the specially authorized operational authority described in that provision. Consult Pub. L. 43–275 for full enacted wording.

notes.heading: Federal Aviation Administration Continuity and Restricted Airspace Act—Direct Amendments to § 106
paragraphs: Pub. L. 43–276, §§ 3(a)–(b), 4(a), 5(c) and 9(a)–(b), expressly amends 49 U.S.C. § 106. Under the enacted amendment, the Federal Aviation Administration is jointly administered by the Department of Homeland Security and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, and its Administrator is nominated by the President with Senate advice and consent.

Pub. L. 43–276 prescribes joint supervision with homeland-security lead responsibility for restricted-flight enforcement, security and protective matters, and NASA lead responsibility for aviation safety, aerospace technical standards and NASA facility-related matters. It preserves presidential resolution of supervisory disputes and provides continuity during vacancies and transfers.

Section 9 directs conforming substitutions of transportation-department references where they concern FAA placement and supervision; its qualifications do not authorize across-the-board replacement of unrelated Department of Transportation authorities. These amendments control over inconsistent preexisting text pending exact USLM subsection-level consolidation. This is an amendment note, not a claim that all prior text in this section has been rewritten.

notes.heading: Restricted Flight Areas—Pub. L. 43–276, § 7
paragraphs: Pub. L. 43–276, § 7(a), expressly adds permanent restricted-flight-area requirements at the end of 49 U.S.C. § 40103. The Federal Aviation Administration must establish, publish, maintain, regulate and enforce restricted areas over the White House Complex, the United States Capitol and Capitol Hill Complex, Joint Base Moore, and covered approaches, protective buffers and surrounding airspace.

The enacted provision governs authorizations, exclusions, security coordination and enforcement responses, while retaining the Department of Defense's operational and using-agency authority for military airspace, including Joint Base Moore. See § 7(a)(i)–(xxiv) of Pub. L. 43–276 for the operative terms and exceptions.
This note identifies the precise amended section; definitional citations to other aviation provisions are not treated as amendments.

notes.heading: Restricted-Airspace Enforcement—Pub. L. 43–276, § 8
paragraphs: Pub. L. 43–276, § 8(d), expressly adds provisions at the end of 49 U.S.C. § 46301 addressing knowing violations of FAA restricted-flight areas, prohibited areas, NASA facility airspace restrictions, emergency orders and lawful operating conditions.

The enacted amendment authorizes civil penalties and administrative aviation remedies, including appropriate suspension or revocation of permissions and grounding orders, and permits referral for criminal prosecution under independently applicable law. Consult Pub. L. 43–276, § 8(d)(i)–(x), for the full scope and standards.
This amendment note preserves the source and precise target pending validated subsection-level consolidation; the note itself does not replace the underlying Code's full text.

notes.heading: NASA Facility Airspace Authority—Pub. L. 43–276, § 6
paragraphs: Pub. L. 43–276, § 6(a), directs an insertion after 51 U.S.C. § 20113 in chapter 201 to authorize the NASA Administrator to establish and manage restricted airspace for NASA facilities and launch, landing, reentry, testing, research, aerospace and facility-security operations.

The enacted provision includes authorization and waiver procedures, coordination with FAA and Homeland Security, and preservation of NASA operational authority. Section 8 of that Act describes the new authority by reference to 51 U.S.C. § 20113A, but § 6 itself does not supply a numbered section heading. Accordingly the exact new-section placement awaits structural verification; no adjacent provision is silently overwritten.
See Pub. L. 43–276, § 6(a)(i)–(xii), for the controlling enacted text.

notes.heading: Homeland Amendment Act—Appointment of Director
paragraphs: Pub. L. 43–277, § 2(a), expressly amends Pub. L. 42–273, § 4(b), which was classified to this section in the 2026 current-law codification.

The replacement text states: “The Director shall be appointed by the President, after consultation with the Secretary of Homeland Security.” Pub. L. 43–277, § 3, makes the amendment effective immediately upon enactment.
This amendment is to the specified appointment clause, not to the other statutory authorities incidentally mentioned in Pub. L. 42–273.

notes.heading: Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court—Renewable Judicial Terms
paragraphs: Pub. L. 43–278, § 3 (first occurrence), replaces § 103 of Pub. L. 30–222, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court Establishment Act. It does not expressly amend the text of a numbered Title 50 Code section; this location retains the prior Act's statutory-note history.

Under replacement § 103(a), the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court continues to consider applications for electronic surveillance, physical searches, data collection and other investigative measures against suspected foreign espionage or terrorism agents or entities. Under replacement § 103(b)(i)–(ii), the Chief Justice appoints no fewer than one United States district judge, who serves renewable six-month terms.
This note states the newer enactment's controlling amendment to Pub. L. 30–222 without treating other Title 50 provisions as amended.

notes.heading: Armed Forces Continuity Act of 2026—Service Activation and Deactivation
paragraphs: Pub. L. 44–279, §§ 3–6, establishes continuing rules for the operational status of military services identified in 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(4), subsequently established military services, and the District of Columbia National Guard. The reference to § 101 is definitional; this Act does not amend the text of that section.

No executive officer, department or agency may activate or deactivate a covered military organization, including by constructive deactivation, except pursuant to an enacted joint resolution under § 5 of Pub. L. 44–279. The President may transmit a proposed change to Congress; Congress may also initiate authorization itself. Existing service operational status otherwise continues.

Section 6(e) preserves the President's command, deployment, organization and operational-employment authority, including changes to subordinate units or commands, provided that authority is not used to circumvent the statute. The Act is effective upon enactment.

notes.heading: Executive Disclosure Act of 2026—Reports to Congress
paragraphs: Pub. L. 44–280, §§ 4–8, requires monthly reporting to designated congressional committees from the Secretary of State, Secretary of Defense, Attorney General, Secretary of Homeland Security, and Director of National Intelligence or authorized designees. The cited department definition in 5 U.S.C. § 101 is incorporated by reference, not amended.

Section 9 permits withholding substantially sensitive information subject to stated justification and committee subpoena authority and preserves applicable privacy, safety, treaty and ongoing-proceeding restrictions. Section 10 imposes up to a $5,000 fine and up to five days' imprisonment for a specified reporting violation. Section 11 makes the Act effective the first full calendar month after enactment.
Pub. L. 44–280, § 3(e), separately repeals Pub. L. 26–188 (Departmental Reports Act) in its entirety. This newer reporting regime supersedes that earlier enactment.

notes.heading: Repeal of Departmental Reports Act (Pub. L. 26–188)
paragraphs: Pub. L. 44–280, § 3(e), expressly repeals Pub. L. 26–188 in its entirety. Any earlier historical or statutory-note presentation of the Departmental Reports Act at this Code location must be read subject to that repeal.
Pub. L. 44–280 supplies a successor executive reporting regime in §§ 4–10. The repeal of Pub. L. 26–188 is not an amendment to every Code section cited in either law.
